paragraphs.text: White is one of the five colors of mana in Magic . A white card is defined as any card with a white mana symbol in its mana cost ( , , , etc) or a white color indicator ( , , etc). White magic is drawn from plains and embodies the principles of morality and order. The white mana symbol is a stylized sun. On the color pie, it is allied with green and blue , and is enemies with red and black . White idealizes peace, believing that there are enough resources in the world for everyone, but this is compromised by selfish desires. Thus, white puts the community above the individual and achieves its goal through tenets of structure: laws, civilization, and morality.

In gameplay, white's virtues of teamwork and balance are represented by its playstyle of deploying small but multitudinous creatures and enacting symmetrical effects that benefit all players (or equalize all players ). As the strongest defensive color, white utilizes a variety of bolstering , life gain , and protection spells to keep its creatures and themselves safe from harm's way, in addition to taxing enemy plans and directly removing any threats such as creatures , enchantments , or artifacts . In addition to being friendly to creatures , white is also proficient at enhancing its army with noncreature spells, such as Equipment and Auras , and dispensing combat tricks , ensuring favored trades that coerce the opponent into lost fights and eventually, a lost game.

Although white can address many different types of threats , white's uncreative inflexibility causes most of its answers to be situational and vulnerable to being answered themselves, such as enchantment removal against white's Aura prison effects. Also, white's morality makes it difficult to outright destroy target creatures, opting for pacifying , lawful defense by removing tapped creatures, or indiscriminate board wipes that reset white's tempo. White's rigidness regarding equality lends itself towards spells that affect all players - which can be abused by opponents - and small, similar-sized creatures that are vulnerable to board wipes. Furthermore, white's bureaucratic organization makes it the worst color at card draw and is limited to effects that usually only draw one card a turn, leading to white languishing with all the prepared tools it needs but without the adaptiveness to have them all at once.
The current member of the Council of Colors for white is Corey Bowen .

White values the group, community, and civilization as a whole. White's ultimate goal is peace, a world where everyone gets along, without disruptions to safety and unity. To govern and protect its community, white uses morality (ethics, religion), order (law, discipline), uniformity (conformity), and structure (government, planning).

White's sense of morality is both firm and unyielding. It does not focus on the individual, but instead on the whole. White encourages individuals to act according to white's goals, but disregards their personal views to preserve the health of the group. White sticks up for the minority and feels that it deserves fairness as much as everyone else.

Strength, fortitude, elegance, and purity are all aspects of white. So is inflexibility: white has an iron will and little room for change. For those who don't share white's values, this can look like fascism, conformism, and oppression.

Believing that individuals are inherently selfish, white suppresses individuals' power. It uses civil laws so that individuals do not disturb the whole with their ambitions (black) or craving for freedom (red). White prioritizes the good of society over the rights and welfare of a single individual. Socialism is a white doctrine, imposing numerous laws that are good for society at large. " The needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few " applies to the white way of living. White quickly suppresses dissent within its ranks.

White creates an entrenched, bureaucratic political system to minimize change. White is typically honest about its goals. It is also defensive, striking only when struck first or when a significant threat is posed. However, it can stretch this belief with the reasoning that a preemptive strike is the best way to defend itself.

To maintain its society, white values conformity and balance. Nonconformity can result in diversity and individuality, which white sees as a threat to unity. Imbalance can likewise threaten unity: if one citizen excels above others, then others might desire to excel, feel inadequate, or fear losing their positions. White's enemies are not expected to play nicely, so sometimes the scales need to be balanced by force.

White is not a prejudiced color. In white's eyes, other colors should be defended against, but not unjustly persecuted. White promotes its own more often than it discriminates directly against anyone (unlike black, e.g., Engineered Plague ). White may even promote its enemies if they happen to share similarities (e.g., Shared Triumph , Celestial Crusader , and radiance ).

White's two main strengths are organization and law. White's ability to organize makes it efficient, as seen in the differences between cards like Leonin Skyhunter and Foul Imp or Veteran Armorer and Sell-Sword Brute , in white's many one-mana removal spells, and its access to board wipes . White is the best color for acting and winning within the legal system. It can also change laws, flavored as enchantment destruction.

Other strengths include white's numbers and its strategies. White motivates large numbers of creatures to fight for its cause (for example, through religion ), allowing it to outnumber its opponents. To white, the loss of one person in an attack is irrelevant if it allows several others to succeed. White is also a great military strategist due to the discipline it implements in its troops. However, its strategies are more defensive than offensive; even maneuvers that support offense are equally useful in supporting defense (e.g., Glorious Anthem and Warrior's Honor ).

White's weaknesses include a lack of appeal to the individual. To compensate for this, it tries to appeal to as many people at once in hopes of them disregarding their self-interest in exchange for the support of the community. White also lacks creativity. It will not tolerate differentiation of any kind and condemns innovation or individuality. This makes white slow to react to new threats. White's rigid structure can also handicap white as much as its enemies.

A common misconception is that white stands for good . White is often good, but not always. Takeshi Konda from the Kamigawa Cycle is a white antagonist, obsessed with bringing his nation glory but losing sight of the individual. White has been an antagonist in the form of law enforcement ( Azorius Senate ), government ( Consulate ), or a cult ( Ojutai ), or as visionary antagonists who commit atrocities for what they believe to be morally correct (Konda, Elesh Norn , and Nahiri ). Its association with the law also allows for "deal with the devil" factions, like the Ravnican Orzhov Syndicate or the Capennan Brokers .

White doesn't always stand for good, except in its own mind. However, when taken to extremes, white's ideals cross the lines of morality. Dictatorships are military institutions and follow strict codes of law placed upon their citizens, though few would call dictatorships "good".
Archons as a whole represent the more negative aspects of white. Broadly speaking, white ties with blue as the second color to have the most antagonists, the first being black.

White has both defensive and offensive mechanics. Both are informed by white's moral sensibilities: it doesn't like to hurt or kill, but it believes that violence is sometimes necessary to achieve peace. Some mechanics, like vigilance, are both defensive and offensive.
The following evergreen keywords are primary in white:
Defender (shared with blue )
First strike and double strike (shared with red )
Flying (shared with blue, black , and red )
Indestructible (shared with black and green )
Lifelink (shared with black)
Vigilance (shared with blue and green )
Ward for mana (shared with blue and green)
^† Secondary in that color.

White's main form of offense is raising an army. A military is an expression of white philosophy: many normal people working together to achieve something greater than the sum of its parts. Because of this, white's aggressive game plan is to flood the battlefield with small creatures ("weenies"). Many white mechanics, such as battalion and the warlord ability, directly reward the weenie strategy. White does still have some larger creatures, like Angels .

White is primary in generating creature tokens , which are usually 1/1s and often created more than one at a time, supporting its small-creature theme. This contrasts with green, the other primary token producer, which makes relatively fewer large (3/3 and bigger) tokens. Examples of white token producers include Release the Dogs and Hare Apparent .
In addition to small creatures, white also cares about cards with low mana values generally. Examples include Ajani, Outland Chaperone and Serra Paragon .

White is one of the most combat -centric colors, so many of its mechanics benefit attacking and blocking. First strike and double strike reflect white's military training, appearing particularly on Soldiers ( Fencing Ace ) and Knights ( White Knight ); these keywords are shared with red , whose fighters informally "train" via brawling. Vigilance allows white creatures to attack and still block, playing both into white's offensive and defensive tendencies; vigilance also evidences the resolute nature of soldiers and other white creatures. Flying is white's main form of evasion ; white fliers tend to be small and efficient, contrasted with blue 's larger fliers. Many white set mechanics, such as exalted , reward a player for having creatures in combat.

The white weenie strategy is supported by anthems , cards like Glorious Anthem that permanently increase the power and toughness of all a player's creatures. Anthems appear primarily in white, where they don't usually exceed +1/+1.

White gets combat tricks to benefit its attacking and blocking creatures. These are usually power and toughness boosts of +1/+1 or +2/+2, and often grant an additional ability; examples include Adamant Will and Fleeting Flight . White can also pump all of its creatures at once ( Inspired Charge ). Combat tricks can exceed +2/+2 when they only affect blockers, as in Righteousness and Hold the Line . White also gets boosting from creature to creature, as with Traveling Minister and Brave-Kin Duo .
White is primary in creating and caring about +1/+1 counters . Examples include Felidar Retreat and Inspiring Paladin .
White is primary in gaining life , with more life gain spells than any other color. This is often flavored as healing, and ties into white's defensive nature and long-term strategic planning.

Life gain comes in several forms, including fixed amounts (as in Angel's Mercy ), scaling amounts ( Archway Angel ), repeatable triggered abilities ( Hinterland Sanctifier ), Food tokens ( Cat Collector ), and bonuses stapled onto other card effects ( Joust Through ). Life total doubling ( Beacon of Immortality ) is exclusive to white, as are creatures with power and toughness dependent on a player's life total ( Serra Avatar ).

Lifelink , one of white's primary keywords, causes life gain whenever a creature deals damage. Lifelink in white is typically flavored as satisfaction or spiritual fulfillment from doing the right thing.

In addition to life gain, white is the only color that gets damage prevention (as in Fleeting Flight ). Damage redirection , a subset of damage prevention ( Vengeful Archon ), is also exclusive to white. Some cards, such as Healing Salve , give the player a choice of damage prevention or life gain.

White reanimation spells, often flavored as healing magic, tie into its defensive, long-term strategy. White is the only color that can reanimate any permanent type. This includes creatures ( Resurrection ), artifacts ( Refurbish ), enchantments ( Silent Sentinel ), planeswalkers ( Onakke Oathkeeper ), and permanents generally ( Profound Journey ). White can reanimate lands with "target permanent" spells, but doesn't normally call out lands. While it can reanimate any creature, it normally only brings back small creatures (often defined as mana value 2 or less), as in Raise the Past . Some noncreature reanimation, like Sun Titan , is also limited to low mana values.

White is also primary in returning creatures or permanents the same turn they go to the graveyard. Some of these cards return the creatures directly to the battlefield ( Brought Back ), while others return the card to hand ( Together Forever ).

White has a suite of tools to protect its creatures from removal and other threats. It is primary in protection , indestructible , and ward for mana ; it's also tertiary in hexproof . Some white creatures naturally have protection, such as Paladin en-vec and Absolute Grace ; most cards that grant protection to a creature are also white. White normally gets protection from black ( White Knight ), protection from red ( Silver Knight ), or protection from a color of the caster's choosing ( Ward Sliver ). There are several enchantment cycles in white that grant protection either to a creature as an aura ( Green Ward ) or as a global enchantment to prevent damage from a source of a selected color ( Circle of Protection: Blue ).

White's protective mechanics also extend to the player . White it can grant a player hexproof. It's also the primary color of " You can't lose the game and your opponents can't win the game ", as seen on Herald of Eternal Dawn .

White is primary in defender (shared with blue ), and even its non-defender creatures have the highest toughness-to-power ratio of any color. White has a minor theme of pumping toughness more than power, as in Holy Strength (contrasted with the black Unholy Strength ). Beginning with Castle ( Limited Edition ), a white toughness-boosting card appeared in every core set through Magic 2014 . Now most white pump spells boost power as much as toughness.

White has the broadest suite of removal spells in the game, able to eliminate any problem permanent except lands . Its removal is often exile -based rather than destruction , flavored as a moral opposition to killing. White is primary in enchantment removal (as enemy enchantments serve to prevent white from having its way ), primary in many forms of creature removal, and secondary in artifact removal; it can also answer nonland permanents generally, including planeswalkers and battles . However, white's removal is limited by its sense of morality and usually comes with a drawback.

Some white removal spells have built-in answers. White can suppress permanents with Auras like Pacifism and Faith's Fetters , and it can temporarily exile them with cards like Banishing Light and Banisher Priest . In both cases, the white removal spell is itself vulnerable to removal. This reflects white's moral scruples: it would rather bind, neutralize, or lock up a threat than destroy it.

Conditional creature removal also reflects morality—specifically, white's desire to justify its violence. White doesn't like dealing the first blow, but it will eliminate creatures who attack , block , or damage white; this extends to destroying tapped creatures, since attacking is the most common way for a creature to become tapped. White can also proactively remove creatures that it sees as threats: those that are black , red , or large (defined as power 3 or greater ). Examples include Take Vengeance , Devout Decree , and Stand Up for Yourself .

White can deal direct damage to creatures in certain circumstances. Sometimes this takes the place of destruction or exile in conditional removal spells, as with Joust Through . White spells can also deal damage equal to the number of creatures controlled by the caster ( Kabira Takedown ), which fits into white's go-wide army flavor.

White can permanently remove a threat while giving back something of value to compensate. Examples of compensation include card draw ( Oblation ), artifact tokens ( Get Lost ), ramp ( Path to Exile ), and life ( Solitude ). When costed low enough, compensatory removal can be the strongest in the game—which warps the color pie , as black is supposed to be better than white at creature removal. Swords to Plowshares exemplifies this problem and is considered a color pie break .

Some white removal lacks any drawbacks. White can unconditionally remove artifacts and enchantments ; examples include Disenchant and Demystify . It also gets unconditional creature removal at high mana values , as with Angelic Edict , although this is a point of contention within R&D .

White is the foremost color of mass creature removal spells like Day of Judgment . This is an outgrowth of white's desire for balance; it doesn't like to discriminate, but treats everyone equally. Resetting the board also flavorfully puts everyone on equal footing, and thus ties into white's themes of justice and fairness. White is also primary in board wipes that only affect creatures with high power, such as Dusk and Elspeth, Sun's Champion , which plays into white's weenie strategy .

Some white board wipes remove permanents other than creatures, such as artifacts and enchantments ( Farewell ) or nonland permanents generally ( Planar Cleansing ). White also has mass land destruction cards like Armageddon ; while Magic in general has moved away from mass land destruction, the effect is still technically in color pie for white.

White is the primary color of tapping opponents' creatures ( Blinding Mage ). White can also untap its own creatures in defensive spells, allowing for surprise blocks ( Village Bell-Ringer ), and gets self-untapping creatures as a form of pseudo-vigilance ( Axgard Braggart ).

White shares flickering —exile a creature, then return it to the battlefield—with blue . As of 2021, R&D has pushed flickering more in white, although it remains primary in both colors. Flicker effects can return the target to the battlefield right away ( Ephemerate ) or at the end of turn ( Charming Prince ). White also gets mass flicker effects like Eerie Interlude and Sudden Disappearance .

White cares more about enchantments than any other color. It sees enchantments as tools for building a better world and as a way to avoid violence and maintain its moral high ground. White typically has more enchantments at lower rarities than other colors. It can animate enchantments ( Opalescence ), return them from the graveyard to the battlefield ( Archon of Falling Stars ) or hand ( Tragic Poet ), tutor for them ( Three Dreams ), copy them ( Ondu Spiritdancer ), and reduce their cost ( Starfield Mystic ), as well as simply rewarding playing as many enchantments as possible with spells like Sphere of Safety and Sigil of the Empty Throne . Some cards care about Auras specifically, such as Ajani's Chosen and Boonweaver Giant .

White is primary in the enchantress ability ("Whenever you cast an enchantment spell, draw a card"), along with green . Following a new rule for white card draw spells, white enchantresses are now limited to one card per turn. Older cards that break this rule, such as Mesa Enchantress , are considered color pie breaks .

White is also primary in caring about artifacts . Its artifact synergies are often restricted to Equipment —flavored as weapons and armor training—and, to a lesser extent, Vehicles . It can tutor for Equipment and Vehicles, put Equipment directly from the hand to battlefield ( Stoneforge Mystic ), and circumvent equip costs ( Sigarda's Aid ). Some cards that care about Equipment also care about Auras, such as Heavenly Blademaster and Open the Armory . General artifact-synergy cards include Bronze Guardian and Ethersworn Canonist .

White cares more about legendary cards generally, and planeswalkers specifically, than any other color. It can tutor for them ( Thalia's Lancers , Call the Gatewatch ), return them from the graveyard ( Yomiji, Who Bars the Way , Onakke Oathkeeper ), and cheat them into play ( Sisay, Weatherlight Captain , Urza Assembles the Titans ). White planeswalker-synergy cards are flavored as calling upon the aid of a planeswalker ally, or as planeswalkers joining forces for the common good.

White is the primary color of taxing effects—preventing an opponent's actions unless they pay a cost , usually mana. Examples of this are Kataki, War's Wage , Ghostly Prison , and Archangel of Tithes . White's use of ward is also a form of taxing. If the taxation cost is high enough that opponents don't have a meaningful choice, as with Smothering Tithe , the card may be considered a color pie break .

White is also primary in setting rules that opponents must follow. It has several cards that restrict when, which and how many spells can be cast ( Rule of Law , Drannith Magistrate , Grand Abolisher , Silence ), which creatures can attack or block ( Ghostly Prison , Blazing Archon ), and which abilities can be activated or triggered ( Hushwing Gryff , Stony Silence ). White features defensive enchantments that punish attackers, such as Teferi's Moat and Worship . It's primary in meddling effects, such as Nevermore , which let the caster prevent a specific card of their choice from being played. And white can benefit from an opponent takes certain actions through cards like Esper Sentinel .
White is primary in exiling cards from the graveyard . Examples include Rest in Peace and Angel of Finality .

White is tertiary in drawing cards . Like all colors, it has access to cantrips —spells which draw a single card, such as Helpful Hunter . White has the best small cantrip creatures (contrasted with green, which has the best large cantrip creatures). White can also draw multiple cards with a single spell, but only once per turn, and only on turns when the player performs an appropriately white action —such as attacking with a certain number of creatures ( Chivalric Alliance ), having creatures enter the battlefield ( Tocasia's Welcome ), or gaining life ( Exemplar of Light ). Once-per-turn draw spells play into white's long-term game plan. They are flavored as white gaining a benefit from following its own laws.

White can tutor for Plains cards, especially when an opponent controls more lands. Some of these "catch-up" cards, such as Claim Jumper and Keeper of the Accord , can put the land directly onto the battlefield, acting as a form of ramp . White is only tertiary in land tutoring, not getting nearly as many land tutors as green .

In black, white sees a foe who spits on moral laws. In white's opinion, black selfishly disregards morals for its benefit and must be vanquished, lest black set a dangerous example for white's impressionable citizens. Black values the needs of the individual over the needs of the group, while white values the exact opposite. White sees catering to individual needs as impractical and wasteful. White also disagrees with black's methods: black's amorality and dishonesty result in underhanded fighting tactics, while white fights with honor and respect. White sees black as deceitful and malignant, while believing itself to be open and honest.

However, white also respects black on several issues. Both colors place an importance on religion; black individuals are not godless, and thus not without aim or sense, unlike red. Black's faith also demonstrates loyalty and a desire for self-improvement, which white can relate to. White respects that black is fighting for the values it believes in. It also respects black's affinity for sacrifice: the grim necessity of death to achieve one's ultimate goal. It understands black's stance in terms of its conflict with green , free will versus destiny, valuing an individual's heroic choices. Although white cooperates with allies and encourages cooperation among its citizens, it shares black's pragmatism and brutality on the scale of nations: for one civilization to win, another must lose. Black's emphasis on self-help can also inform white's desire to care for individuals, especially when friends are involved.

White sees red as an enemy that does not respect civil laws and does as it pleases, without regard for the rules or well-being of the community. Red is unnecessarily aggressive, and its brash actions often leave white's citizens injured, homes burnt, and crops ruined. White will not tolerate this. In combat white favors strategy, structured ranks, and planning; red prefers not to plan and to strike without warning before the opportunity leaves. Red claims to be an advocate of freedom, which white views as chaos. White believes that if red is free to express its radical and selfish emotions, it will incite similar emotions within white's community, leading to unrest or insurrection. To achieve peace and order within white's community, the forces of chaos must be destroyed.

However, white respects red on some shared similarities. Red is driven, its followers are willing to die for their cause; white's followers can be equally zealous, proudly dying in the name of religion or morality. Unlike black, red respects the power of numbers and the group. Red also has a "strike first, ask questions later" mentality that white can understand. White values emotion, wanting to show its followers that it cares for them. White is also aware of the dangers of inaction and realizes that to achieve peace, it must prepare for war — truths that red embraces. As such, most white-red cards deal with combat abilities; nearly all white-red keywords ( first strike , double strike , battle cry , battalion ) are combat abilities.

White and green are allied against their common enemy, black . Black disregards harmony; it values the need of the individual and, at its worst, selfishness. White and green agree that life and harmony are important. White also enjoys the idea of an agrarian society, which employs many of white's citizens while feeding everyone, extending white's selflessness to a concern for nature. Green also values other white ideals, such as peace and tranquility, which white strives toward. White and green both seek order, though in different forms. White can see that green cares as much for the denizens of the forest as white is concerned about its people. Green also puts as much emphasis on spirituality as white, though it is more free-form than white's religion.

Although they're allies, green and white clash over thinking versus feeling. White believes that green should spend more time thinking about its actions and not acting brashly. Green acts based on instincts (which white sees as synonymous with emotion), which heeds no law and knows nothing of morality. Green would rather have a fun party than die for a noble cause. This disparages white, for which law and morality are fundamental. If green were to have its way, only the strongest and the fittest would survive, and the weak and those with no natural purpose would be consumed; this goes against white's interest in giving everyone a fair chance, no matter their size. White is also more concerned with the law in the abstract. White can be dogmatic and hard-nosed, which tends to step on green's toes. While green appreciates the protection and safety that the law affords, it isn't interested in the subtle bureaucracy that comes with it. Green is only concerned with law and morality as long as they apply to everyday life.

White and blue are allied against their common enemy, red . Red fights for personal freedoms and the right to express its emotions. White and blue find common ground in thought, planning, discipline, self-restraint, and rules, so they both view red as at threat. White agrees with blue's thoughtfulness; its recognition of the importance of law, structure, and rules; and its ability to plan for the future, all of which it views as useful for society. Blue would prefer things to be done in a quiet, neat, and orderly fashion; it may lack the warmth that white would occasionally like to display, but white is willing to compromise to control its citizens. White seeks peace, and blue seeks prosperity; together, they act for what they believe is the common good.

White and blue do not always see eye-to-eye. The conflict between the two is interdependence versus parasitism. White works with the community for it to prosper and succeed, but blue sees the community as merely subjects to be observed and notes to be recorded. The people are a means to acquire the knowledge blue seeks, and it's not concerned about them beyond that, and this upsets white. White also believes that blue should be more actively involved and open about its projects, but blue is secretive and often deceitful, which makes white even less comfortable. Blue also sees value in the individual and in doing things (and keeping things) to itself, but white feels that putting any value in the individual can only serve to devalue the group. Blue also puts the most importance on facts, data, and solid information, which makes it the most scientific (and thus arguably the most secular) color. White values religion, which inspires zeal and purpose while maintaining moral and civil order; white fears that if blue were to have its way, the community would abandon religion altogether.
